title: TankieTube
text:
TankieTube was a five-day collaborative research sprint at the University of Amsterdam. Our team compared “natively digital” Marxist-Leninist YouTube creators with formal political organizations.
Project leads: Gavin Mueller and Ema Kinsel.
Team: Luca Ghiselli, Ada Paul, Sean Ryan, and Jo Walton.
My part focused on the Tenet/Rumble comparison, and I also helped make the final poster. This was my first real hands-on exposure to Google Colab, very large text datasets, and computational internet research.

title: TankieTube
text:
Project poster




Open poster in new tab ↗

title: TankieTube
text:
Tenet/Rumble comparison
I found a public dataset of 560 Tenet Media videos on Rumble and compared its transcripts with the much larger Tankie corpus.






ImportantWhat this comparison does not show



This is an exploratory text-similarity analysis. Similar language does not demonstrate coordination, ideological equivalence, causation, or support for “horseshoe theory.” The analysis instead looks for places where speakers with very different political motivations arrive at overlapping rhetoric, framings, or conclusions.



TF-IDF surfaced important words shared across both datasets.
“Israel” became a focus, and a sentence-similarity matcher paired Tenet quotes with the closest Tankie quotes.

The goal was to identify rhetorical convergence that would be difficult to spot manually, including cases where different ideological reasoning produced similar framings or conclusions.

title: TankieTube
text:
What the team found
The broader dataset covered 23 YouTube channels, nine political organizations, ~2.4 million YouTuber comments, ~107.4K organization comments, and over 6,000 hours of audio.

The YouTubers and formal organizations focused on noticeably different topics.
YouTubers appeared more shaped by platform dynamics, while organizations looked more like traditional social-movement activism.
The team also found some aesthetic convergence between older organizations and newer YouTube-driven Marxism-Leninism.

title: TankieTube
text:
Why it mattered to me
Five days of working inside datasets that were far too large to read manually made computational research feel much more concrete. It helped push my interests toward digital investigations and data-driven online research.

title: Lyon Cycling Map
text:
While studying abroad in Lyon in summer 2025 as a Gilman Scholar, I recorded bicycle rides with a GoPro and used the footage’s GPS data to reconstruct the routes and turn them into an interactive map.
This was my Gilman Scholarship Follow-on Service Project, designed to document Lyon’s cycling infrastructure and make the city easier for future students to explore.






Open the map in Google My Maps ↗



The basic workflow was:

Record rides around Lyon with a GoPro.
Extract the GPS coordinates associated with the footage.
Organize the location data into usable routes.
Load the routes into Google My Maps to create an interactive view of where I had ridden.




This was my Gilman Scholarship Follow-on Service Project while studying abroad in Lyon, France. I recorded my rides, extracted the GPS coordinates from the footage, organized the routes, and turned them into an interactive map that other people could explore.
I like this project because the data came directly from something I was doing in the real world. It was an early example of using data and mapping to document an experience and make it useful to other people.

title: All We Are Solar Map
text:
I built this interactive map for All We Are, a Raleigh-based nonprofit working with communities in Uganda. The goal was to turn a spreadsheet of solar installations into something people could explore visually instead of reading through rows of project data.

Project status: This page preserves the version I built before ongoing maintenance was handed off to the All We Are team. The map and bundled CSV here are a project snapshot and may not reflect the nonprofit’s current installation data.







Open the full interactive map ↗ · View the map repository on GitHub ↗



The map reads a CSV export from a read-only master sheet I built. That sheet pulled the fields needed for the map from four existing All We Are spreadsheets into one view without modifying the organization’s source data.
Visitors can:

browse solar installation locations across Uganda
use a customer/site selector to jump directly to a location
zoom into clustered areas
click a site to see details such as installation date, number of systems, customer type, district, and population
switch between map styles




The project is a small Mapbox GL JS + D3 application. D3 loads and parses the exported CSV, while Mapbox handles the interactive map, clustering, navigation, and popups.
The workflow was: four source spreadsheets → read-only master sheet → CSV → interactive map. The master sheet referenced the organization’s existing data rather than changing it. At handoff, a fresh CSV export could replace the map’s data file. This repository now keeps the last bundled CSV as a reproducible snapshot of the version I worked on.



One of my favorite parts was building the master sheet itself: pulling useful fields from four separate spreadsheets into one clean, view-only layer for the map without touching the original records.
The project is a good example of the kind of technical work I enjoy: taking information that already exists inside an organization and making it easier to understand and use.

title: ClearHouse.live
text:
ClearHouse.live was a collaborative winter project built to make U.S. politicians’ financial disclosures easier to search and understand.
It was also my introduction to web scraping, public-records data collection, and building a data-backed web application.



  

Open ClearHouse.live ↗



The site organizes politician stock trades from Periodic Transaction Reports and financial disclosures into a searchable public-facing platform.



This was the first project where I had to think about the whole pipeline instead of just a finished dataset:

finding and collecting public disclosure data
extracting useful fields from filings
cleaning and storing transactions
connecting the data to a web interface
checking the source documents when automated extraction looked wrong

That experience is what eventually led me back to congressional stock disclosures with the newer House and Senate PTR pipelines.



The project uses Python/Flask, SQLAlchemy, SQLite, HTML/CSS/JavaScript, and Chart.js, with background processing for financial-disclosure data and external market-data services.



ClearHouse was the project that made public-records data feel like something I could actually build around. It connected politics, scraping, data cleaning, and web development in a way that stuck with me.

title: Park it here? E-bike and scooter rules differ across NC State
text:
TECHNICIAN
      View original on Technician ↗
    
    
      News
      Sports
      Opinion
      Culture
      Multimedia
    
  

  
    
      
      
      
      X
      
      
    

    
      
      Sean Ryan, Correspondent • Sep 11, 2026
      

      NC State enrolled 39,259 students in fall 2025, continuing a three-year trend of record enrollment. By contrast, parking capacity has remained essentially flat at around 20,000 spaces for the past decade.
      Parking access was already strained last fall, when limited spaces and a lottery system left many students relying on luck to secure permits. This lack of parking may have manifested in micromobility options becoming more popular around campus.
      Nicole Odell, who earned her Ph.D. in Parks, Recreation and Tourism Management from NC State, researched e-scooters and active transportation on campus, studying how students were using Spin (a shared electric bike and scooter rental service) on and around campus.
      In a 2024 post-trip survey, nearly half of respondents whose trips started or ended at NC State were undergraduates living on campus.
      “I think more mobility choices are better to get people around,” Odell said.
      The need for alternatives is especially relevant for newer students, who are lower on the credit-hour priority list for parking permits, and may have to find other ways to get to and around campus.
      In the age of phone apps, Spin and Lime have helped fill that gap by providing access to electric bikes and scooters.
      However, GIS data reveals vastly different experiences for riders depending on whether they choose Spin or Lime, the two major app-based bike and scooter rental services available around NC State. Spin is NC State’s contracted micro mobility provider, while Lime operates through its partnership with the City of Raleigh.
      That split means riders can encounter different parking and service-area rules depending on which app they use, creating a potentially confusing experience for students unfamiliar with the two systems.
      As NC State’s contracted micromobility provider, Spin operates under a different arrangement on campus than Lime, including a campus-specific rate the University calls the “NC State Rate.” Pricing was one factor considered during the University’s request-for-proposal process, where companies offered their rates for the campus community.
      Gabrielle Bubin, University transportation planner and TDM coordinator, said rates for rides differ based on location and destination.
      “So you’ll see on the Spin app currently that for students that start rides that originate from NC State’s campus, it starts at $1 to unlock and 30 cents [per minute],” Bubin said. “That would look different if you were in Durham, per se.”
      The maps show a major difference between Lime and Spin at NC State. Between Main and Centennial campuses, the two companies use different no-parking restrictions, with Lime heavily restricting where riders can leave scooters and e-bikes.
      Map legend
      
        Blue: Service area where scooters and e-bikes can operate
        Solid red: No-parking zone
        Red stripes: No-ride zone; riders cannot pass through
        Gray: NC State campus areas
        Green: Bike routes physically separated from traffic
        Yellow: Bike routes using painted lanes or shared roads
      
      
      Lime’s rideable area also does not extend to the Centennial Biomedical Campus, meaning riders cannot use Lime to travel to or around it. Spin, meanwhile, explicitly includes a separate service area for the Biomedical Campus.
      
      Parking restrictions may also affect the different streets riders use. If students can’t park near their destination, they may have to keep riding until they reach an allowed area, which could be on streets shared with cars.
      Odell said even one difficult connection can make an otherwise usable route feel unsafe.
      “I think a lot of it comes from not feeling safe on a road,” Odell said. “If you think of outside of campus, like if you’re trying to get to or from campus, the connections, your whole network has to feel safe because one nasty intersection can keep somebody from making that bike trip, even if everything else is reasonable.”
      N.C. Department of Transportation crash records from March 2015 through 2025 show 168 reported crashes involving bicyclists, scooters and other cyclists within 2.5-mile-diameter areas centered on NC State’s Main, Centennial and Centennial Biomedical campuses. The bicycles on the map mark the location of each reported crash.
      The data doesn’t show whether Lime or Spin riders were involved, or whether geofencing — virtual boundaries that control where bikes and scooters can be ridden or parked — played any role, but they provide context for the traffic environment riders may face when parking options are limited.
      
      
      These restrictions may become more important as NC State grows and more students look towards alternative transportation to get around campus. In the next five years, NC State is projected to lose up to 2,000 parking spaces with the demolition of the older portion of Coliseum deck.
      NC State also permanently removed on-street parking along Morrill Drive and is using the space to build dedicated bike infrastructure. These planned bike lanes along Morrill Drive, running beside Carmichael Gym, will give students a safer and more separated route to reach campus amenities and move between different parts of campus.
      As parking and driving become a more limited option to students, bikeshare use is increasing. Raleigh reported more than 5,500 e-bike trips in September 2025 alone, almost as many rides in one month as the city saw during the entire first half of 2025 with its old docked bikeshare program.
      The growth of bikeshare also brings its own set of problems. Bikes and scooters left in inconvenient or improper locations can block paths and create problems for people moving around campus.
      Demar Bonnemere, communications manager for NC State Transportation, said riders and pedestrians can use the Spin app to report a poorly parked bike or scooter.
      “The biggest thing is to either let us know [at the NC State Transportation office] or send a notification directly through the Spin app, and then we’ll get somebody out to relocate the device into a proper area,” Bonnemere said.
      Even with the growing pains, bikeshare systems are adding to the transportation options that students can use to get around campus.
      For Odell, those options are also part of a larger question about how dependent students should have to be on cars.
      “You need a place to live, you need to get around, you need transportation, but it shouldn’t have to be that you need to have a car,” Odell said.

title: Political Text Analysis
text: How does Donald Trump’s Iran-related Truth Social rhetoric change in the day before, day of, and day after UCDP-recorded U.S. or joint U.S.–Israel conflict events, and is threat language elevated beforehand?

title: Political Text Analysis
text: How does Donald Trump’s Iran-related Truth Social rhetoric change in the day before, day of, and day after UCDP-recorded U.S. or joint U.S.–Israel conflict events, and is threat language elevated beforehand?

title: Political Text Analysis
text:
Data
Two sources are aligned by date:

Trump’s Truth Social posts. The full public archive of his original posts (not reblogs) is pulled from a Hugging Face dataset, filtered to calendar-year 2026 and to posts mentioning Iran (401 posts YTD as of this snapshot).
UCDP conflict events. The Uppsala Conflict Data Program’s Georeferenced Event Dataset, filtered to events with US or joint US–Israel involvement related to the Iran conflict (through July 2026). UCDP is manually researcher-coded from primary reporting on organized violence, which makes it a more reliable “ground truth” for event timing and severity than automated event trackers like GDELT, though its inclusion rule (battle-related fatalities) means it can miss purely diplomatic or political moments that don’t involve violence.

For each UCDP event, a 1-day event window (day before / day of / day after, in Eastern time) is built around it, and any Iran-related Trump posts falling in that window are attached. This produces 393 unique event-dates with matched posts, spanning 543 underlying UCDP event records.
Each event-date is also assigned a significance level (Standard, Notable, High, Major, or Context) from same-day UCDP record count, best fatality estimate, and civilian death count — e.g., 2026-02-28 and 2026-04-06 are both coded “Major” based on same-day death tolls in the dozens to low hundreds. The exact rule is below.

title: Political Text Analysis
text:
Significance levels
The central event circle and the clickable bottom timeline in the visualization are both sized and colored by this classification, derived directly from the UCDP event workbook:


Minor: another same-day UCDP event date.


Notable: same-day best estimate ≥ 5, or at least 2 same-day UCDP records.


High: same-day best estimate ≥ 10, or at least 3 same-day UCDP records.


Major: same-day best death estimate ≥ 25, or same-day civilian deaths ≥ 10.


Multi-day Event: a multi-day record begins on that date, but there is no same-day fatality record to assign to that specific date.


The intent is to visually emphasize dates with more substantial same-day UCDP activity, without assigning an entire multi-day fatality total to the first day of a long record.

title: Political Text Analysis
text:
Approach

Collect Trump’s Truth Social posts (Hugging Face archive) and UCDP’s Iran-conflict event records (filtered Excel export), both refreshed periodically as new data becomes available.
Window the two datasets together: for every UCDP event, pull Iran-related posts from the day before, day of, and day after.
Score rhetoric with zero-shot classification. A Hugging Face multi-label zero-shot classifier (facebook/bart-large-mnli) scores each post’s content_text — and only the text, never the UCDP metadata — against six categories: Threat, Victory, Diplomacy, Ceasefire/Ending, Blame Allies, and Media Criticism, each receiving a continuous 0–1 entailment score.
Aggregate event-balanced means. Because posting volume varies a lot day to day, scores are first averaged within each event, then averaged across events — so a single high-volume posting day doesn’t dominate the pattern.
Visualize the result as a connected, per-event timeline: each UCDP event sits at a central node sized/colored by significance, with the day-before/day-of/day-after posts and their six rhetorical scores branching around it. Each post is also tagged with its single dominant category as a small colored badge.

title: Political Text Analysis
text:
Rhetorical category guide
The six categories are multi-label: the model evaluates each one independently, so a single post can score highly in more than one category. In computational text analysis these are often called rhetorical “frames,” but this page uses category as the plainer label. The values are model entailment scores, not calibrated probabilities.
Each card below is the highest-scoring post for that category among the 87 unique posts in the current 26-event analysis subset. The full archived post is shown directly in the card, followed by that post’s scores across all six categories and a link to the original Truth Social post.

Military threats, escalation, retaliation, ultimatums, warnings, strikes, or destruction directed at Iran.

title: Political Text Analysis
text:
Results

Open the timeline in its own full-width page ↗ — recommended on desktop, since the embed below is narrower than the page it’s showing and falls back to the mobile layout.






The interactive timeline above shows, for each UCDP event, the surrounding Trump posts and their per-post Threat/Victory/Diplomacy/Ceasefire/Blame Allies/Media Criticism scores (plus a small badge showing that post’s single dominant category), and a summary comparison of event-balanced averages across the day-before/day-of/day-after windows. The timeline itself is responsive: on wide viewports (like the standalone page above) it shows the full connected rail with day-before/day-of/day-after branches side by side; on narrow viewports (including this embedded version, since its column is narrower than the 900px breakpoint) it collapses into a tab switcher instead.
The clearest evidence for telegraphing: average Threat language is actually higher the day before a UCDP event (0.55) than on the event day itself (0.52) or the day after (0.48). It’s also visible in individual posts — in the day before the April 6 event (34 killed in strikes on Iran’s Guards intelligence chief and a university), Trump wrote: “Tuesday will be Power Plant Day, and Bridge Day, all wrapped up in one, in Iran. There will be nothing like it!!!” — naming the target categories before further strikes happened.
Blame Allies and Media Criticism were added as later passes after the first four labels. Blame Allies (criticizing NATO/European allies for not helping) is low overall but ticks up on the event day (0.13) versus the day before (0.07) and day after (0.11). Media Criticism (attacking press coverage as biased or fake) varies a lot post-to-post (from near 0 to near 1) but doesn’t move much across the three windows (0.34–0.35 throughout) — a real, variable signal at the post level that just isn’t specifically tied to event timing. (A different sixth label, Self-Credit, was tried and dropped earlier — it scored near-ceiling on almost every post regardless of timing, which made it more a constant feature of the voice than a useful signal.)

title: Political Text Analysis
text:
Limitations

Small sample. 87 unique posts are scored across the 26 events shown here (many event-windows have no matching Trump post at all), and results should be read as a descriptive pattern within one leader’s rhetoric during one specific conflict, not a generalizable claim.
Zero-shot labels are heuristic. The classifier was never fine-tuned on this domain; label probabilities reflect a general-purpose model’s association between text and label names, not a validated measure of intent or sentiment.
UCDP’s fatality-based inclusion criterion means the event set may under-represent diplomatically significant moments (sanctions, negotiation breakdowns) that didn’t involve violence — so “no nearby UCDP event” doesn’t mean “nothing happened.”
No counterfactual baseline. This only looks at posts already inside event windows — it doesn’t compare day-before Threat language ahead of strikes against day-before Threat language on dates where no strike ultimately happened. Without that comparison, elevated day-before Threat could reflect genuine advance signaling, or it could just be Trump’s ordinary baseline level of threatening rhetoric during an active conflict, which happens to precede strikes only because strikes were frequent during this period.
Both the Truth Social archive and the UCDP extract are periodic snapshots (current through mid-2026), not a live feed; this page will be refreshed as new data comes in this semester.
